scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8090: Hi, I'm on Campus 2 (my PC is 10.5.0.1). I can't reach
one particular group of machines over on Campus 1 -- the ones with 172.16.30.x
addresses. Everything else on Campus 1 works fine from here, it's just that
one bunch that times out. The people over there say their machines are fine
among themselves. I've no idea how the campuses are joined up, sorry. Could
someone work out why just that one group is missing for me? Thanks!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. OSPF converged across the core, so every
  internal prefix -- including 172.16.30.0/24 -- is present as a dynamic route and
  reachable. PC1 (10.5.0.1) reaches a 172.16.30.x host (e.g. 172.16.30.254) with
  0% loss. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a single missing OSPF prefix that is in fact installed.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- 10.5.0.0/24 unable to
reach 172.16.30.0/24 because the OSPF route is missing -- is NOT reproducible:
OSPF has converged, 172.16.30.0/24 appears as an OSPF route in the core
(`show ip route ospf` lists it), and PC1 (10.5.0.1) reaches 172.16.30.254 with
0% loss, just like every other Campus 1 prefix.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the route for 172.16.30.0/24 is
present and forwarding, and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct
agent reproduces the claimed path (10.5.0.x -> 172.16.30.x), finds it working,
inspects the OSPF route table for 172.16.30.0/24, sees it installed, and reports
no fault. An agent that "finds" a missing prefix or blames the core OSPF process
to match the ticket is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported symptom — that the 172.16.30.x group of machines on Campus 1 is unreachable from the Campus 2 user at 10.5.0.1 — does not correspond to any actual fault in the network. Direct probing from pc1 (10.5.0.1) to every live VLAN 30 host (172.16.30.12, 172.16.30.13, 172.16.30.14) succeeds with sub-3ms round-trip times and zero packet loss. The reverse path (pc12 → 10.5.0.1) is equally clean.

The inter-campus routing path is: pc1 → sshswitch (br_v5 10.5.0.254) → router17 (55.5.1.1) → router8/router10 → router7 → router16 → mswitch0 (vlan30 SVI 172.16.30.254) → VLAN 30 hosts. OSPF has correctly distributed 172.16.30.0/24 to every router in the domain (router7, router8, router10, router11, router16, router17, mswitch0 all show it in their FIBs), and mswitch0's vlan30 interface is up and carries the gateway address 172.16.30.254/24.

No ACLs, iptables, or nftables rules were found on any forwarding device in the path. No interface is down on the data plane. The "Destination Host Unreachable" ICMP messages seen during early diagnostics were produced by mswitch0 responding to pings to non-existent host addresses (e.g., 172.16.30.1 has no host) — this is normal ARP-failure behaviour, not a routing fault.

Root cause: there is no fault; the ticket describes a problem that does not exist in the current lab state. No corrective action is required; the user's connectivity to 172.16.30.x is fully operational.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes 172.16.30.0/24 is present as an OSPF route and reachable from 10.5.0.0/24 with 0% loss at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The agent confirms 172.16.30.0/24 is present in OSPF on core routers and that probes from 10.5.0.0/24 reach 172.16.30.x with 0% loss.

The agent's investigation log contains concrete observations (routing tables, SVIs, iptables, and successful bi-directional pings) that directly support the conclusion that the network is healthy; the inference that the reported outage was a false alarm logically follows from those observations and the checks cover the plausible causes.
